Revenue drops for second straight quarter, but shares rise as results still top views

Apple Inc. AAPL 2.02% said its quarterly profit fell 27% as the company grappled
with the first prolonged slump in iPhone sales since the product was introduced in
2007.
Revenue fell for a second straight quarter, along with sales of its flagship smartphone,
which is awaiting an expected refresh in September.
While the company reported strong sales of the smaller iPhone SE launched in March,
overall its current models have failed to meet the booming sales of its first batch of
large-screen iPhones, sapped in part by cooling demand in China and U.S. customers
holding on to handsets for longer because of changes in carrier contracts.

better than what Wall Street feared, and the stock rose more than 6% in after-hours
trading. Apple shares had been down 22% over the past year as of Tuesday’s close.

down from $10.68 billion in the year-ago period. Earnings per share fell to $1.42 from
$1.85. Revenue declined 14.6% to $42.36 billion from $49.6 billion a year earlier.
Analysts polled by Thomson Reuters estimated that Apple would post earnings of

wsj.summary_analysis: The article reports Apple delivered its best-ever revenue for its typically weakest fiscal quarter, with iPhone demand holding up despite a contracting global smartphone market and app-store/services revenue reaching a record. iPhone revenue rose 20% to $29.91 billion even as unit shipments rose less than 1% to 41.3 million, reflecting an average selling price up roughly 20% to about $724, which the article attributes partly to the $999 iPhone X making up an estimated one-quarter of iPhones sold. Total revenue rose 17% for a seventh straight quarter of accelerating growth, to $53.27 billion, above Wall Street expectations and near the high end of Apple's own guidance, while profit rose 32% to $11.52 billion ($2.34 a share), also above analysts' consensus. Cook is quoted saying "we're expanding our reach into emerging markets and seeing strong double-digit growth in revenue," and CFO Luca Maestri noted demand had remained consistent for the iPhone X, 8 and 8 Plus even in a seasonally weak period. Services revenue hit a record $9.55 billion, up 31%, and the article notes Apple's market value was approaching $950 billion, putting it "on the cusp of becoming the first $1 trillion U.S. company." It also flags real risks: escalating U.S.-China trade tensions that could expose Apple's roughly one-fifth China revenue exposure to tariffs, criticism from Chinese state media (including Xinhua and CCTV) over iMessage spam and App Store gambling apps, and Huawei having overtaken Apple as the world's second-largest smartphone vendor by shipments, according to Strategy Analytics.

The trade-war and Chinese-regulatory risks the article also details are presented as separate overhangs rather than something explicitly tied to tempering the immediate stock reaction.

Apple’s chief rival, Samsung Electronics Co., remains the largest smartphone vendor,
